name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,165

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: 25 being one of his characters

blocks.note: the answer to 25 down, Mr Dick of David Copperfield
ens is the philosopher's Latin word for a being or entity

explanation.surface: A remark that the fool at 25 is one of a certain novelist's creations.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the novelist's name is literally Dick plus a word for being, and Mr Dick is one of his characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens created Mr Dick, so the novelist is the man whose character the entry at 25 is.

clue.text: Note the children in this fictional Yorkshire village

blocks.note: do is a note of the sol-fa scale
taken as written
boys are male children

explanation.surface: Pointing out the young pupils of an invented Yorkshire village.
explanation.walkthrough: Dotheboys Hall is Wackford Squeers's brutal school in Nicholas Nickleby; the name, 'do the boys', mocks how it cheats its pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: The school stands in the made-up Yorkshire place that gives it its name in Nicholas Nickleby.

clue.text: Game will we hear involve hop-grower

indicators.note: we hear means as spoken, so the sound of the words counts, not their spelling

blocks.note: the board game chess plus will contracted, said together

explanation.surface: A game that, word has it, will draw in a hop farmer.
explanation.walkthrough: In David Copperfield, Chestle is the hop-grower who marries the eldest Miss Larkins; the name is said 'chessel'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Chestle in David Copperfield is a Kentish hop-grower, the man who wins Miss Larkins.

clue.text: Assembled under one church; Tappertit thought there were bounds to his

definitions.text: Tappertit thought there were bounds to his

indicators.note: assembled means put together in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of under rearranged
an means one
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A congregation gathered under one church, and Sim Tappertit's limited patience.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Tappertit in Barnaby Rudge complains that there are bounds to human endurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the capacity to put up with things, which Tappertit says has limits.

clue.text: Where Mrs Jarley's penurious poet might live

definitions.text: Where Mrs Jarley's penurious poet might live

blocks.clueFragment: Where Mrs Jarley's penurious poet might live
blocks.note: surface reading: the sort of poor district a needy poet would inhabit
setter's reading: the poet's own name is also a word for such a district

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Jarley runs the travelling waxworks in The Old Curiosity Shop; her hack poet, who writes her advertising verses, shares his name with a squalid area.
explanation.definitionFit: A rundown, overcrowded urban district is where a poor writer would lodge, and it is also Jarley's poet's name.

clue.text: How Monks described Oliver, as brat ill-used by Dodger initially

indicators.note: something ill-used is knocked about, so these letters are thrown out of order
initially points to the opening letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
first letter of Dodger

explanation.surface: Oliver Twist, abused by the Artful Dodger, insulted by his villainous half-brother Monks.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oliver Twist, Monks is Oliver's half-brother and scorns him as illegitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver was born out of wedlock, and Monks repeatedly calls him by the insulting word for an illegitimate child.

clue.text: Flirtatious maidservant harassed by stalker about entrance to chamber

indicators.note: harassed means troubled and agitated, so the letters are thrown about
entrance to points to the first letter of the word after it
about means surrounding, so the jumble wraps round the single letter

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
first letter of chamber

explanation.surface: A flirty maid pestered by a stalker lurking near her room.
explanation.walkthrough: Betsy Clark is a minor Dickens character, a coquettish servant girl; the stalker is only surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The character is a housemaid given to flirting, so a coquettish servant girl.

clue.text: 'Tis perhaps what John Hutley did with the patient all night

definitions.text: what John Hutley did with the patient all night

blocks.note: surface reading: an archaic 'it is' opening a sentence
setter's reading: the answer read as an instruction, a word meaning be seated written upwards as in a down entry, produces this word

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, taken as wordplay in a down light, says to write a three-letter verb upwards, which gives 'Tis. In The Pickwick Papers, John Hutley watched over the dying clown through the night.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay awake through the night tending someone ill is exactly what Hutley did beside the dying pantomime clown.

clue.text: Monks found here mostly in best type of reasoning

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: A1 means first-rate, the 1 read as I
a priory is a house of monks

explanation.surface: Monks are in Oliver Twist, but this describes the best reasoning found among monks.
explanation.walkthrough: Monks, a character in Oliver Twist two clues earlier, is here just monks in a religious house.
explanation.definitionFit: A priori reasoning argues from first principles to consequences, deducing before experience.

clue.text: Gullible ones ruined by Dodson yielding term in prison

indicators.note: the term of a word is its end, so the last letter is taken
yielding means giving up, so the letter is surrendered from the name
ruined means wrecked, so what is left is rearranged

blocks.note: Dodson of Dodson and Fogg, the lawyers in The Pickwick Papers
last letter of prison

explanation.surface: Naive clients fleeced by the lawyer Dodson, then a stretch in the Fleet prison, as in Pickwick.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodson and Fogg's suit sends Mr Pickwick to the Fleet prison, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodos is informal for stupid, easily fooled people, after the extinct flightless bird.

clue.text: Register at start of "Tale …" that the Woodman's was muffle

indicators.note: start of points to the opening letter of the title word that follows

blocks.note: first letter of Tale
a meter registers or reads a quantity

explanation.surface: A literary note on the opening of A Tale of Two Cities, where the Woodman Fate works with a muffled step.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as published ends 'muffle'; the quotation is 'muffled tread'. In A Tale of Two Cities the Woodman (Fate) and the Farmer (Death) work silently, with muffled steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A tread is a footstep, and Dickens says the Woodman's footsteps were muffled.

clue.text: Turned out badly like Betty Higden's mind

indicators.note: badly suggests the words come out wrong, so their letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sad verdict on how Betty Higden's thinking developed.
explanation.walkthrough: Betty Higden in Our Mutual Friend is a poor old woman who cannot read; 'Turned out badly' reads like a comment on her life.
explanation.definitionFit: Betty Higden had no schooling, so her mind was uneducated, never taught by anyone.

clue.text: What's revealed by Dolly Varden, tirelessly thorough

indicators.note: what is revealed by some words is already lying within them, waiting to be uncovered

blocks.note: surface padding: completes the character's name, Dolly Varden
spans the end of Varden and the start of tirelessly

explanation.surface: Dolly Varden, the coquette of Barnaby Rudge, tirelessly showing all.
explanation.walkthrough: Dolly Varden is the flirtatious locksmith's daughter in Barnaby Rudge.
explanation.definitionFit: Entire and thorough both mean complete, with nothing left out.

clue.text: Sensations making Tappertit audibly stomp about

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the sound of the name counts, not its spelling
about suggests moving things around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Simon Tappertit of Barnaby Rudge is called Sim
the letters of stomp rearranged

explanation.surface: Simon Tappertit stamping around causes a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Tappertit, the swaggering apprentice of Barnaby Rudge, is known as Sim.
explanation.definitionFit: Symptoms are bodily feelings that signal illness, so sensations is a fair synonym.

clue.text: "… the — of oysters alone are not gregarious" (American Notes)

definitions.text: "… the — of oysters alone are not gregarious" (American Notes)

blocks.clueFragment: "… the — of oysters alone are not gregarious"
blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a word missing
setter's reading: supply the missing word from Dickens's American travel book

explanation.walkthrough: In American Notes Dickens observes that in American oyster cellars the eaters of oysters keep to themselves, unlike everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means the people who gulp oysters down, i.e. those eating them.

clue.text: "The howling — of tabular statements" (Hard Times)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a word missing
setter's reading: supply the missing word from the quotation in Hard Times

explanation.walkthrough: In Hard Times Mr Gradgrind's statistics are a howling sea of figures; the missing noun is a five-letter expanse of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens likens the mass of statistical tables to a vast stormy sea in the passage quoted.

clue.text: Comfortable miser discomfited in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: discomfited means thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: comfortable, as in well-off
the letters of miser rearranged

explanation.surface: A well-off miser upset, put in terms of how he talks.
explanation.walkthrough: Sam Weller of The Pickwick Papers coined comic sayings of the form 'as the man said when...', named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a type of humorous saying, a particular way of expressing things, after Sam Weller's habit.

clue.text: Briefly medicated one badly, like Smike at the end

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped
badly suggests things done wrong, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, then shortened
a means one

explanation.surface: Smike, at the close of Nicholas Nickleby, treated poorly with medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: Smike, the ill-treated boy of Nicholas Nickleby, wastes away and dies of consumption.
explanation.definitionFit: Emaciated means abnormally thin and wasted, as Smike becomes in his final decline.

clue.text: City businessman becoming a lord in an Oxford college

indicators.note: in places the small pieces inside the college name

blocks.note: Merton is an Oxford college
taken as written
Ld is the abbreviation for lord

explanation.surface: A City man ennobled and set up at an Oxford college.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Malderton is the social-climbing City man in the Boz sketch Horatio Sparkins; the City is London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Malderton made money in the City of London, so he is the businessman of Dickens's sketch.

clue.text: Turner perhaps, name of 25

blocks.note: first meaning: one who swivels, i.e. turns
second meaning: the surname of Dick in The Old Curiosity Shop

explanation.surface: J. M. W. Turner the painter, apparently identified as someone called Dick.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner looks like the painter, but it simply means something that turns. Dick Swiveller is the clerk in The Old Curiosity Shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A swiveller is literally one who pivots or rotates, and Dick Swiveller carries that surname.

clue.text: How Mrs Hunter described a dying amphibian? Quite the opposite!

definitions.text: How Mrs Hunter described a dying amphibian

blocks.clueFragment: How Mrs Hunter described a dying amphibian
blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: in poetry, as Mrs Leo Hunter wrote her Ode to an Expiring Frog
second meaning: reversed, contrary

explanation.surface: A poetess's dying frog, and then a cry that the truth is the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pickwick Papers Mrs Leo Hunter composes the Ode to an Expiring Frog; split as 'in verse', the answer describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inverse means opposite or reversed in order, while split in two it says the ode was written as poetry.

clue.text: Answer to what "The Chimes" may give – a watery ring

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
chiming bells sound a toll

explanation.surface: A riddle about what Dickens's Christmas book The Chimes provides, solved with a ring of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chimes is one of Dickens's Christmas books, but here it is just bells ringing.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a lagoon, so a circle in the sea.

clue.text: What Mr Crisparkle climbed at Cloisterham Weir, exposed to the air

definitions.text: What Mr Crisparkle climbed at Cloisterham Weir

blocks.note: out means exposed, revealed
an air is a look or appearance

explanation.surface: The Minor Canon of Edwin Drood scrambling up at the weir, out in the open air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposed to the air' looks like one phrase; split it. Crisparkle, the athletic canon of Edwin Drood, searches the weir where Drood's watch is found.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlook is a high vantage point for viewing, the sort of place one climbs to look out over a river.

clue.text: Father Jack, guest in the Haunted House

definitions.text: Jack, guest in the Haunted House

blocks.note: first meaning: old slang for one's dad

blocks.clueFragment: Jack, guest in the Haunted House
blocks.note: second meaning: Jack, the narrator's cousin who stays in The Haunted House

explanation.surface: A priest called Father Jack staying in a haunted house.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Jack looks like one priest's name, but Father is a separate definition. The Haunted House is a Dickens Christmas story.
explanation.definitionFit: Governor is informal British slang for one's father or boss, and also Jack's surname in the story.

clue.text: How greengrocer yawned in front of Mr Tuckle (about page 500)

definitions.text: How greengrocer yawned in front of Mr Tuckle

indicators.note: about suggests turning round, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of page rearranged
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A citation of the Bath footmen's soirée in The Pickwick Papers, as if to page 500.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like a page reference, but it holds the wordplay. Mr Tuckle chairs the footmen's 'swarry' in Pickwick, where a greengrocer waits at table.
explanation.definitionFit: To have gaped is to have stared open-mouthed, the way the greengrocer yawned before Tuckle.

clue.text: Over which twisted housebreaker fled, otherwise retreating from society

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the word is read from the end

blocks.note: or introduces an alternative, otherwise
of can mean from, as in made of or born of
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: Bill Sikes the burglar, fleeing and cut off from society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twisted housebreaker' is Bill Sikes of Oliver Twist, who flees over the rooftops of Jacob's Island and dies there.
explanation.definitionFit: Sikes escapes across the tops of houses, so these are the coverings of buildings he runs over.

clue.text: Tiny Tim shortly to tell about description of Oliver's friend, name of 25

definitions.text: description of Oliver's friend, name of 25

indicators.note: shortly tells us to cut the name short by its final letter
about suggests turning things around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then its last letter dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tiny Tim and Oliver Twist's friend gathered in one Dickensian sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiny Tim' looks like one name, but Tiny is the definition. In Oliver Twist, Oliver's workhouse friend is called Little Dick; 25 is DICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Little means tiny, and is also the word attached to Oliver's friend Dick.

clue.text: Surname of fool recurrently occupied by Charles's head

definitions.text: Surname of fool recurrently occupied by Charles's head

blocks.clueFragment: Surname of fool recurrently occupied by Charles's head
blocks.note: surface reading: a simpleton whose name is taken over by a king named Charles
setter's reading: the David Copperfield simpleton whose memorial keeps being invaded by thoughts of King Charles I's head

explanation.walkthrough: Mr Dick, Betsey Trotwood's harmless lodger in David Copperfield, can never finish his memorial because King Charles the First's head keeps getting into it. 'Charles's head' also tempts the solver towards Dickens's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentle simpleton in David Copperfield goes only by this surname, as Mr ___.

clue.text: Pegler is confused about part of oratorio he composed

indicators.note: confused means mixed up, so the letters are rearranged
about means going round, so the jumble wraps around the single letter
part of takes just a piece of the word, here its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
first letter of oratorio

explanation.surface: A man called Pegler muddled over a section of an oratorio he wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: Pegler looks like a person, but is just letters to rearrange. Pergolesi wrote the Stabat Mater and oratorios.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Battista Pergolesi was an 18th-century Italian composer, the man who composed the oratorio.

clue.text: Lachrymose manservant has no hesitation in identifying lover of Miss Manners

indicators.note: has no tells us something is missing from the name, so letters are removed

blocks.note: Job Trotter, Jingle's tearful servant in The Pickwick Papers
er is a hesitant sound

explanation.surface: A weepy servant names, without pausing, the man courting Miss Manners.
explanation.walkthrough: Job Trotter weeps on demand in The Pickwick Papers. Alexander Trott courts Julia Manners in the Sketches by Boz story The Great Winglebury Duel.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Trott is the suitor who ends up eloping with Miss Julia Manners in the Boz sketch.

clue.text: Medic with letters describing what Mr Sapsea does at the Dean

definitions.text: describing what Mr Sapsea does at the Dean

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
esses are the letter S, written out in the plural

explanation.surface: A doctor with letters after his name describing Mr Sapsea's behaviour towards the Dean.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edwin Drood, the pompous auctioneer Mr Sapsea copies the Dean's style; Dickens says he 'dresses at' the Dean, i.e. models his dress on him.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress at someone is to imitate their clothes, which is what Sapsea does to resemble the Dean.

clue.text: Children's family like the gloves that Kenwigs sent out for

definitions.text: like the gloves that Kenwigs sent out for

blocks.note: kids are children
kin is family

explanation.surface: The Kenwigs family and its children, linked to some gloves Mr Kenwigs ordered.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kenwigses are a genteel family in Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidskin is soft leather from young goats, the material of the fine gloves Kenwigs sends for.
